checkpoints.line: Blocks dangerous domains and links before a device ever connects.

materials.what: Every link starts with a lookup: your device asks for a name like bank.example before it can open the page. Cisco Umbrella checks that name first, against threat intelligence from Cisco Talos, and blocks known phishing and malware sites before any connection is made. In the game that's the harbour: a look-alike sender or a fake link should never get a boat into town.
withoutLines: One click can hand over a password
Nobody sees which links were risky
withLines: Known bad domains are blocked at the lookup
Phishing pages never load
The team sees every blocked request
materials.realWorld: Someone at school gets a message from "bank-supp0rt" and taps the link. With Umbrella the lookup is blocked, the fake login page never loads, and the security team sees which device tried to reach it.
materials.learnMoreLabel: Cisco Networking Academy: Introduction to Cybersecurity

checkpoints.line: Decides which doors are open, and for whom. Anything else is dropped.

materials.what: Every service on a network listens on a numbered door, its port: 443 for secure websites, 23 for Telnet. Cisco Secure Firewall checks each connection against access control rules, from the top down, and the first rule that matches decides. Anything no rule allows is dropped. In the game you're the rules: open only the doors the town needs, only for the people on the list.
withoutLines: Old doors like Telnet stay open
Anyone can knock on any door
withLines: Only the doors the town needs are open
Rules say who may use each door
Everything else is dropped
materials.realWorld: A company keeps its website open on 443 for everyone, lets staff use other services only from inside, and keeps Telnet (23) shut, because it sends passwords as plain text. Anything else that knocks is dropped and logged.
materials.learnMoreLabel: Cisco Networking Academy: Introduction to Cybersecurity

checkpoints.line: A second check on your own phone, so a stolen password isn't enough.
checkpoints.with: A second step on your phone

materials.what: A password is one factor: something you know. If it's stolen or guessed, it opens everything. Cisco Duo adds a second factor, something you have: after the password, the owner approves the login on their own phone. Attackers try push bombing, sending approval after approval until someone taps Yes, so Verified Duo Push asks for a code shown on the login screen. If you didn't ask to log in, deny it and report it.
withoutLines: A guessed password opens the vault
Stolen logins look like the owner
withLines: The owner approves on their phone
A stolen password alone fails
Verified Push asks for a code
materials.realWorld: A student's password leaks from an old game site. The attacker tries it on the school account, but the approval goes to the student's phone. They didn't ask, so they deny and report it, and the account stays safe.
materials.learnMoreLabel: Cisco Networking Academy: Introduction to Cybersecurity

checkpoints.line: Protects every device and catches malware, like a fake update.

materials.what: Updates fix the cracks attackers use, so real ones should go in fast. But a fake update is one of the easiest ways to slip malware onto a device. Cisco Secure Endpoint checks files on laptops and servers, watches how programs behave, and can quarantine a suspicious file or isolate an infected device. In the game: check the signature and the sender before you fit anything.
withLines: Suspicious files are checked
Malware is detected and stopped
The team can see every device
materials.realWorld: A pop-up offers a "free speed boost" from a site that isn't the real maker. Secure Endpoint flags the file as malware and quarantines it before it runs, and the team can see which device downloaded it.
materials.learnMoreLabel: Cisco Networking Academy: Introduction to Cybersecurity

checkpoints.line: Every decision in town is logged. Splunk searches all of it at once.

materials.what: Every system writes a log: who knocked, on which door, what was allowed. One log alone says little. Splunk, part of Cisco since 2024, collects the logs from every system in one place, and a search runs across all of them at once. That's how a slow scan shows up: one address trying door after door, too quietly for any single house to notice. This is threat hunting, the daily work of a SOC analyst.
withoutLines: Each house keeps its own logs
withLines: Every log lands in one place
One search shows the scanner
The trail leads back to the source
materials.realWorld: A security team sees nothing odd on any single server. One Splunk search across all the logs shows the same address probing port 8080 hundreds of times overnight, and the trail leads straight back to it.
materials.learnMoreLabel: Cisco Networking Academy: Introduction to Cybersecurity

checkpoints.line: Split the town into lanes so one infected pod can't reach the vault.

materials.what: On a flat network every device can reach every other one, so one infection can spread everywhere. Cisco Catalyst switches can put groups of devices into separate lanes called VLANs. Traffic stays inside its own VLAN, and anything crossing between lanes has to pass through rules that decide what's allowed. This is segmentation: one infected device stays in its own lane.
withoutLines: Every pod can reach the vault
withLines: Pods sit in separate lanes
An infected pod stays in its lane
Rules decide what crosses lanes
materials.realWorld: A school puts guests' phones, students' laptops and the servers with marks and records in separate VLANs. When a guest's phone is infected, it can't reach the servers, because no rule lets guests cross into that lane.
materials.learnMoreLabel: Cisco Networking Academy: Introduction to Cybersecurity

checkpoints.line: Sees inside every cable: which link is losing packets, and why.
checkpoints.without: The call freezes, nobody knows why
checkpoints.with: The broken link shows up pink

materials.what: When a video call freezes, the problem could be anywhere along the path: the Wi-Fi, the router, the internet provider, or the app itself. Cisco ThousandEyes measures every hop of the path: packet loss (data that never arrives), latency (delay) and jitter (uneven delay), even across networks you don't own. The team fixes the link that's actually failing, instead of guessing.
withLines: Loss and latency shown per link
The bad link is found first
The call is moved to a good path
materials.realWorld: A school's Webex lessons keep freezing. ThousandEyes shows the loss starts at one link at the internet provider, not inside the school, so the team calls the provider about that link instead of replacing the Wi-Fi.
materials.learnMoreLabel: Cisco Networking Academy: Introduction to Cybersecurity
